Hello, I recently wrote a message about proving that the free : Type u ⥤ GrpCat functor preserves monomorphisms. This got me to the following problem: HasZeroMorphisms GrpCat is not in mathlib (not that I know of). AddCommGrpCat proves this in Mathlib/Algebra/Category/Grp/Preadditive.lean, but I don't know where the equivalent for GrpCat would need to be. I guess it would be something like:

instance {G H : GrpCat} : Zero (G ⟶ H) := ⟨ofHom 1⟩

instance : HasZeroMorphisms GrpCat where
  comp_zero f G := rfl
  zero_comp X {Y Z} f := by
    ext x
    exact map_one f.hom

Would a PR like this be useful?

For AddGrpCat, a HasZeroMorphisms instance would make sense (even though, this category is probably not used a lot), but otherwise, I doubt we want to speak of the "zero" morphism between two groups that are denoted multiplicatively. If there is a use in order to prove certain theorems, it could be a definition that is not a global instance. Otherwise, I would think that showing that the trivial group is a zero object would be better (if we do not have this already).

Joël Riou said:

For AddGrpCat, a HasZeroMorphisms instance would make sense (even though, this category is probably not used a lot), but otherwise, I doubt we want to speak of the "zero" morphism between two groups that are denoted multiplicatively. If there is a use in order to prove certain theorems, it could be a definition that is not a global instance. Otherwise, I would think that showing that the trivial group is a zero object would be better (if we do not have this already).

There is indeed an instance for HasZeroObject GrpCat in Mathlib\Algebra\Category\Grp\Zero.lean (with its corresponding AddGrpCat.hasZeroObject), and this in Mathlib\CategoryTheory\Limits\Shapes\ZeroMorphisms.lean:

/-- A category with a zero object has zero morphisms.

It is rarely a good idea to use this. Many categories that have a zero object have zero
morphisms for some other reason, for example from additivity. Library code that uses
`zeroMorphismsOfZeroObject` will then be incompatible with these categories because
the `HasZeroMorphisms` instances will not be definitionally equal. For this reason library
code should generally ask for an instance of `HasZeroMorphisms` separately, even if it already
asks for an instance of `HasZeroObject`. -/
@[implicit_reducible]
def zeroMorphismsOfZeroObject : HasZeroMorphisms C

If it's ok, I will create a private instance of HasZeroMorphisms GrpCat
I do not think that proving that the free group functor preserves monomorphisms requires using a HasZeroMorphisms instance in GrpCat.

I was just generalizing the proof for AddCommGrpCat in the same file (Mathlib\Algebra\Category\Grp\Adjunctions.lean)

instance : (free.{u}).PreservesMonomorphisms where
  preserves {X Y} f _ := by
    by_cases! hX : IsEmpty X
    · constructor
      intros
      apply (IsInitial.isInitialObj free _
        ((Types.initial_iff_empty X).2 hX).some).isZero.eq_of_tgt
    · have hf : Function.Injective f := by rwa [← mono_iff_injective]
      obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := hf.hasLeftInverse
      have : IsSplitMono f := IsSplitMono.mk' { retraction := g }
      infer_instance

Do you think there is a simpler proof?

It seems this uses IsInitial.isZero which depends on HasZeroMorphisms, but if we know there exists a zero object, then it should not be hard to show that an initial object is also a final object, which is what is evnetually used in the proof.
Thanks a lot! I will try to prove that
